name: Jaina Proudmoore
aliases: Proudmoore (Sylvanas, to others and, in chapter 3, shouted at the well)
a Kirin Tor apprentice (Sylvanas's thought, ch3)

physicalDetails.detail: Young even for a human, with lingering roundness in the face. Fair hair once braided, mostly loose. Blue eyes rubbed red at the rims. Bruise-dark shadows under the eyes in the cell lamp.
Brown wool travelling robe kilted up for walking, hem stiff with dried mud. Good boots cracked across the toes; the left retied with a different knot.
Knuckles red and raw, skin split and peeling with frost-nip; right-hand fingers black-violet with ink in every crease.
Staff: plain ash, grain dark from hands, silver wire in close turns on the grip, hen's-egg-sized crystal that goes dull violet under the damper.

Voice scraped thin from talking since before dawn; neck stiff from holding her head tipped back in the chair; knees stiff as dried rope after a day seated. Loose hair she pushes off her forehead with the heel of her hand. Mud to the knee. Ears go hot when embarrassed, and her face colours from the collar up.

Right hand goes numb after deep reads: skin sticks to the dirt and peels when lifted from the frosted road; fingers clumsy for hours, 'pins first, then the burn, then an ache in every knuckle'. Right hand dead again after the frost-sheet cast during the ambush. Left hand left bare for reading the doe.
Staff jammed across the stomach on the first gallop leaves a bar of ache across her middle. After the doe she is wet to the shins and red to the elbow with blood.
Not much of a rider ('never anything at all at this pace'); sits a borrowed mare, left hand wound in the mane at the gallop. Dozes upright in the saddle at dawn and jerks awake.

Chapter 3, seen from Sylvanas: face 'the colour of tallow' in the last light; right hand still dead and tucked up 'useless in her armpit', staff jammed across the saddle-bow under it on the spook. Left hand now also ruined: at the well it tears skin off four fingertips and the heel of the palm onto the frosted stones; three fingers raw and shining; at the storehouse she leaves skin on the boards again and the fingers curl only halfway, 'stiff as a dead bird's foot'. Both hands then wrapped in strips of somebody's linen by Cyndia (palms up in her lap, held against her chest). Cannot close her fingers on a water-skin strap. Carries the staff in the crook of her elbow. Face goes white to the lips after reads and a greenish tinge round the mouth at dawn; swallows repeatedly (nausea). Needs Lyriel's help to mount (Lyriel holds the far stirrup). Ears go red at the tips when Sylvanas says the Kirin Tor ink is 'in your file'. Sleeps upright in the saddle by mid-morning, chin on chest, wrapped hands slack on the pommel, and wakes badly at the noon water.

Chapter 4 (her own POV): right hand still dead ('something she had been asked to carry for someone else'), staff riding in the crook of that arm; left hand wrapped in linen and throbbing, frost coming through the wrapping in a white crust across the knuckles by dusk; left fingers curl only halfway and only two tips are usable for knots. At the granary something 'gave' low in the left palm; in the deep of the night Lyriel cuts off the black-red stiff linen and finds a split in the heel of the hand 'an overripe plum, shiny with the cold'; it is washed and rebound with the fingertips left poking out. Arm 'ice from the fingers to the shoulder' after the shell ward. Slept before arrival (print of the stirrup buckle on her cheek, 'a clear head for the first time since Dalaran'), then wears down again over the night vigil: cold in the roots of her teeth, chest cold under the bodice 'a wet shirt'.

Chapter 4: mounts and dismounts badly every time (staff slides in the elbow, right leg fails to clear the cantle); Lyriel takes her weight at the waist or gives a cupped-hand step. Needs Lyriel's hand under the elbow to rise from her knees; back cracks when she straightens. Green in the face and swallowing at the copper taste. Ears go hot when she is embarrassed (in the lane after Sylvanas handles Brask). Lyriel fastens her cloak at the throat because the left hand cannot manage a clasp. At the end of the vigil the hum goes out of her hands, the left wakes 'in pins and then in burning'.

Chapter 5 (seen from Sylvanas's POV): face 'the colour of the dust' at the first depot, comes down off the mare on Lyriel's arm and walks 'as if the road had gone soft under her', staff heel knocking every second step; staff propped in the crook of the dead right arm, steadied by the two working fingers of the wrapped left hand; two bare fingertips out of the linen, inked from writing and picking at 'a crust of frost' off a fingertip. Cold comes into a room with her, a draught where there is none; her teeth chatter and white frost rises on the two bare fingertips during the fork reading; the staff's crystal runs a washed-out gold going dimmer over the day, 'dull gold, the colour of old horn' at the river depot, brighter at the fork where the light leans toward the bend. Slept sitting, wrapped hand held up off the straw. Grey in the face each crossing and 'a shade less' recovery each time; the mare went down on its knees on the causeway with her still on it, Lyriel caught her arm. Eats the crust Lyriel saves her in two fingers. Pushes hair off her face with the back of her wrist. Gets up on a mounting block with Lyriel's hands under her boot.

Chapter 6 (her own POV, absolute): slept sitting against a stone block with her cheek on a bench end, right shoulder stiff with cold; right arm dead and holding the staff against her ribs ('the one thing it was still good for'); reins in the left hand, wrapped by Lyriel in linen to the wrist with two fingertips bare, palm throbbing in time with the mare's walk, the split in the palm pulling when she grips; Lyriel's burnt crust still in her back teeth. Staff crystal 'the colour of straw left in the rain' (was good clear gold in Dalaran), light dipping each time the road's weight comes up. Cannot feel Arthas's gauntlet on her right sleeve. Spits sour into the mist and wipes her mouth on her own shoulder because she has no hand to spare. Lyriel lifts her down and up at every stop; mud to the ankle at the camp. Bare fingertips go white gripping the unfolded sheet; sour metal taste in the mouth. On the Andorhal approach: teeth chattering in the heat, sweat down her back under her coat, white frost on the bare fingertips with rime creeping over the linen edge, pressure like deep water on her head, ears hurting, the crystal sinking until she can see the grain of the stone, a nosebleed (warm on her lip; the linen came away red with a white hen-feather stuck to it). Wipes her lip with the back of the wrapped hand. Rides sideways-unwilling on a mare that shies; she is a poor rider and knows it.

Chapter 7 (seen from Sylvanas's POV): right arm dead, staff in the crook; holds the pass up between two bare fingertips; jaw shut so hard a muscle jumps under her ear; the linen on her left hand stiff and rust-coloured across the knuckles where she wiped her lip on the hill; blood dried in her nose; chin level. In the arch's shade her lip draws back from her teeth 'as if the air had an edge on it'. At the post she sits on Corin's stool with the staff heel on the earth floor, eyes half shut; later stands by the bench rather than sit, the bench right behind her knees. After the sample room: face grey to the lips, voice hoarse and spent carefully, the crystal at the head of the staff giving no light, the two bare fingertips white to the first joint with frost furred on the linen around them on a warm night. Lyriel's hand under her left elbow and Corin on her dead side.

voiceMarkers.detail: No on-page dialogue in chapter 1. Her only reported words: 'the leylines are wrong' (via the runner); she told the night watch the stones were sick from the inside and wardens only read outsides; asked whether she could be bound at the stone.

Aloud to Sylvanas she is formal and always uses 'Ranger-General'. Under pressure she waters her explanation down to homely images (damp creeping up a wick, rot in a cellar, a river over its banks) and apologises for jargon; the real vocabulary (lattice, resonance, residue, source or sink, lags in the pulse) comes out only once she stops talking down, in her Antonidas register.

Dry self-deprecating humour surfaces when tension breaks ('Then I'll try to go on taking it better than a Ranger-Lord. It seems the least I can do for Quel'Thalas.'). Short clipped answers when afraid: 'Yes.' 'Clear.'

Interior curses and prayers: 'Oh, Light', 'Light help her', 'Light, why won't she go down?'. Interior metaphors are nautical (her father's crews and flagship, hull stove in, pitching deck) and academic (first-year sent back to his bench, cracked crucibles at the Violet Citadel, anatomy slabs, a dowser's hazel fork), with a courtly aside (King Terenas's autumn hunts).

Chapter 3 aloud (the real register, no talking down): urgent and precise when pushing for a read ('Ranger-General, it's right under us. If I put my hand down here now, before it's full dark--', 'It's strongest *here*.'); plain and unembarrassed in failure ('I don't know. I told you on the road I would. I'm sorry.'); carefully structured, evidence-first argument against the loudest answer ('a store is where things end up... Which came first, I can't, not from this. If I tell you it started here and it came from a day's ride off, you'll ride the wrong way, and so will I.'). Practical requests ('Water first. Would you?', 'Louder than last time, please.'). With the child she drops to a low, slow voice, 'pitched down nearly as low as Neral's', and asks single, open, short questions ('Was it before she was ill, the sweetness? Or after?', 'How did you know?', 'Which way were the toes pointing?', 'Every night, or one night?') and 'Thank you.' Quiet dryness with Sylvanas: 'They'll know that in Silvermoon.'

Chapter 4 to villagers: short, plain, warning-first. To Tobin: 'It's a fever. There's something else in it too.', 'Small. Half a fist. A fist. Everywhere. Those will do.' (she hears herself and thinks Antonidas would have had a fit). To patients: 'I'm going to look at you. With a light. It won't hurt you. You might feel warm.', 'You did nothing wrong.' In the lane she has a full Kirin Tor speech ready ('a contamination of the currents, necromantic in character') and shuts her mouth because of the child; her thanks to Brask comes out higher than intended. In the report to Sylvanas she chooses the real register over small words, in sorted order and fast ('It starts in the gut... What sorts them is bread... I can't get further than that from in here.'). Asks the night shutdown of Sylvanas low and in her own formal register ('Ranger-General. The baker lights his oven before light... I can ward a room. I can't ward a village.').

Chapter 4 interior: 'Brilliant, Jaina.', 'Lovely. Write that in the report.', 'Oh, Light.', 'Light help her.'; swears once with a word from the Kul Tiran gunners. Metaphors: Kul Tiran (bowline, sheet bend, clove hitch, breeching ropes, the bosun, reefs off Tiragarde, silt in a harbour, planking on a hull, seams caulked, the Boralus quay mill, the Boralus cathedral reliquary), Dalaran (the alchemy-room flask ward, the locked shelf and grille, Antonidas building a ward), and domestic (a blanket over a cough, a girl in a house with too many lamps and one taper, a fly in old honey, ink in water, a bowl over a candle, cooling jam). Says 'Again' to ask Lyriel to re-teach rather than let it be done for her.

Chapter 5 (heard through Sylvanas): level, brief and plain, no lecture. 'Where do you want me?', 'Yes. It's better there than in a yard. Everything in a yard gets walked over.' Reports in single words and short strokes: 'Heavy. Old.', 'Light.', 'Starting.', 'Nothing.' 'North road's heavy. All the way out, as far as I can hear, and old... East is light. It's only starting.' Pushes back dry and honest: 'Or I'm wrong.' 'I can't tell you what's in a book, Ranger-General. I can tell you the east road is light.' 'Count them, then. I haven't the breath to argue about currents in a shed.' 'I can't hear paper, Ranger-General.' Corrects herself without ceremony: 'I said light at the time, I know. I hadn't heard the rest of the road. Make it heavy.' Similes now domestic: 'Like a room where somebody's smoked a pipe for years, after you've opened the windows.' Dry on Barov: 'talked about wheat all the way through dinner while my father pretended to listen.' Laughs (short, surprised, then properly) at Lyriel's joke ('He put a loop on the seven. On the seven.'). 'Ranger-General' every time aloud; 'Then I'll have to show it to them.'

Chapter 6 aloud: the plain line to Sylvanas ('It's one thing. The flour, the jar, Millhaven. Somebody built it to ride in the grain... It comes in on the wagons and walks out on its own feet.'); honest limits ('I can't tell you who, or how it gets from a knot under a man's breastbone to his feet walking after he's dead.'); dry in company ('Then he can come with me to a granary and watch. I'll find him a jar.'). Formal with the sergeant ('Jaina Proudmoore, of Dalaran. Apprentice to the Archmage Antonidas. I've come to see Prince Arthas. He knows me.'). With Arthas the 'old voice' comes out: teasing, warm, quick ('He'd have to find me first. Look at you, though. They've given you a whole hill, Your Highness, and somebody to polish you.'), then direct ('Arthas, I need you to listen to me, all the way to the end.'), then faster and higher as he turns to the hills; she keeps it short and ordered, and stays careful about Barov ('I'm saying nothing about Lord Barov, only that the grain goes through Andorhal.'). Afterwards plain and level to Sylvanas ('You were right. At the fork.'). Polite to the lieutenant and the tally-man ('Thank you, sir. You've been very kind.'). Answers Sylvanas's question honestly and briefly ('Nothing but a tired clerk.'). Interior: 'Oh, Light.' (twice), 'Oh, it was working.' Metaphors: Dalaran (the locked grille, a master's fire-rules voice, laying a ward with every seam closed, writing a thing up for Antonidas), Boralus (diving off the end of the quay after a sailor's coin), a first-year on her feet with her mouth open before a master.

Chapter 7 (heard by Sylvanas): at the gate, the flat, answered-a-great-many-forms tone: one word at a time ('Dalaran.' 'Yes.' / 'None.' / 'No.' / 'Until the business is done.'), chin level, waits the clerk out. 'My escort.' to cut off the clerk's question about the Ranger-General. At the post: plain and exact ('Thank you. Jaina Proudmoore, of Dalaran. A man on the road, a tally-man from the granaries, told us to ask here for Captain Havel.'); asks Corin questions as if filling a form ('Who did you write to? In Dalaran.', 'Did anyone answer?', 'Can I put my hand on them?'). After the sample room: hoarse, spends her voice carefully, plain load-bearing sentences ('It's put on the grain. A coat, too thin to see.'). Dry about her own limits: 'I tried. Then I talked, and he wrote.', 'I'll know what's in the bags. I won't know who put it there.', 'I've read enough sacks.' Says 'Ranger-General' aloud; 'Captain' to Havel; 'Corin' to Corin.

beliefs.belief: The ward-stones are sick from the inside and the elven wardens will read them sound because they only read the outsides.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Corroborated by Sylvanas's palm (one stone) and by what Jaina hears in the cell stone. Wards also appear to muffle the contamination (ch2).

beliefs.belief: The contamination travels along the leylines from Lordaeron northward and has turned up in the ward-stones through the currents.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Partly wrong. Her hand on the road shows it has left the lines and is in clay, water, roots and living wood; Sylvanas shows the ruled lines all converge on Millhaven, so direction (source or sink) is open. Chapter 3: the crossing read does not settle it.

beliefs.belief: She is competent and the Kirin Tor are too slow ('Eventually. Once they'd agreed what to call it'); Antonidas is 'always too slow, until it turned out he'd been right to be slow'.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Open. She knows he will probably turn out right again and she would still have gone.

beliefs.belief: 'Death-aligned' was a clever phrase for the hitch in the lines; the thing is a residue in the currents.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Overturned in the field: she sees it putting milk in a doe's eyes and keeping her on her feet after a heart-shot. It is physical, lethal and active in living flesh.

beliefs.belief: The loudest site is not necessarily the first: a store (the storehouse by the mill) is where things end up; she will not call it the origin from loudness alone.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Method, not a hidden theory. Chapter 3 never overturns it and never confirms grain or the storehouse as source.

beliefs.belief: The dead of Millhaven are carrying the contamination heavier in their prints than the surrounding ground, and cattle, dogs, hares and wheel ruts are light.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Established by repeated staff reads in the lane and the cut; she wants 'one of them' to test whether they were alive when they walked.

beliefs.belief: The horses are clean and she does not understand why ('They've walked through it all day and drunk out of the stream at the culvert, and it isn't in them').
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Re-checked and confirmed clean at night in the inn yard. Mechanism unexplained.

beliefs.belief: The spread is wider and thinner south of Millhaven ('A stain in a cloth that's been wet through') and 'it's ahead of us... down the road'.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Noon read at the gravel crossing; plan leaves the next village 'alive enough to misunderstand' what is happening to it.

beliefs.belief: If she finds the entry route fast enough she can stop this village becoming another Millhaven (she arrives sure and cheerful, then the drag under the market noise sobers her: 'quieter because it was still moving... because it still had somewhere warm to go').
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Held: the village lives because they are on time and Brask acts on their word.

beliefs.belief: The contamination enters by the mouth, carried in one flour (bread, sops, bakehouse loaves, store sacks); the dose is cumulative and sorts the sick (Garran: bread morning and night for months, everywhere; cooper's house: two loaves a day, a fist and more; Col: two nights of bread after a summer of his mother's oats, a walnut; Mother Haw: her own oats from her own field, well).
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Established by her patient pattern and then confirmed by the jar and the stencilled sacks. It is not water (three houses on one well run worst to best), not contact (Garran, worst case, lives alone), not grain generally (oats are grain).

beliefs.belief: She can ward a room but not a village; wards hold the drag and the door (nothing more comes in, nothing in goes further) but do not cure.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Holds. Only stopping the dose changes the outcome; at dawn the early cases are 'more than holding' and Garran is unchanged.

beliefs.belief: The substance in the jar was built, not found: a stack of at least three spells laid on each other ('one part to keep, one part to wait, one part that did something under the other two that she could not follow'), written in the necromantic grammar the Kirin Tor keep behind the grille. It is also beautiful, and she wants to take it apart.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Stands as her read; the third part is lost when the loft boards burn. Authorship (who built it) unknown: 'Somebody very good made this.'

beliefs.belief: Telling villagers the true name of the thing ('necromantic') in front of a frightened child would do harm; the thing to say is what to do.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Held; she lets Sylvanas speak to Brask and gives the real name only to Sylvanas.

beliefs.belief: If she had frozen Tam to the neck, or the jaw, he might have lived; she is not sure she would have done it ('She had hated doing it to a wolf. And he'd have thawed in the end and sat in the cage... waiting.').
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Open. A guilt she holds privately through the night; the poison was in his collar either way.

beliefs.belief: A road can be listened to from a crossing: heavy = old and settled, light = only starting, a stretch of road 'is better to listen to than a yard'; a read from a mile-post is reliable enough to rank roads.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: So far borne out against Corley's book (north oldest, east nine of ten short-rate loads in the last month) and against Cyndia's counts; but she mis-places marks (Hollow Green put on the first name she came to; Ashford 'not light') and corrects them.

beliefs.belief: The contamination isn't in all the granaries: 'It isn't in the granaries. Or it isn't in all of them.' It goes in on the road, or at the far end, before Andorhal, and comes round the back.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Hypothesis, open. Cannot say which from the table. Her map shows it stacked along the south road, older toward the bottom, with a thin new layer on top.

beliefs.belief: The King's road is clean ('thin... Nothing's ever sat on it'); the south road is heavy, with a new thin layer on old, 'going the same way'.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Staked as her read at the fork ('As sure as Brent's.'); unverified; she offers a re-read from the first bridge and is told no.

beliefs.belief: The paper itself is empty ('It's only paper. It never sat by any of it.'); the ruined waybills carry no residue.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Stated as observation at the river depot. Presumably true; the contamination stayed with the grain, not the books.

beliefs.belief: Cannot say whether the plague started at Millhaven: 'It started there, or it started there first. That's not the same.'
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Open; consistent with Chapter 3 'source or sink'.

beliefs.belief: The plague is one thing, made in parts, every part with a job (carts to carry it, mills and bakehouses to put it in bread, people to eat it a little at a time, the jar's keeping part to hold it whole inside them until enough has gathered, then death, then the body walking). Not bad luck, not a mould, not a fever, not one clever man with a grudge: too many hands, too clean, running on flour and finishing on its own.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Her settled read at the end of the opening beat; stated aloud to Sylvanas. Ladder stops short: she cannot say how a knot under the breastbone becomes feet walking after death. 'That's the part of the jar I couldn't read.'

beliefs.belief: Whoever built it was taught in Dalaran: it is built the way she was taught to lay a ward (every seam closed, nothing loose for the next spell to catch on), and it uses the death-currents craft kept behind the library grille. 'Someone she might have borrowed a pen from on the library stair.'
beliefs.trueOrFalse: A fear, not a finding. She runs down faces (masters, senior students, those who left and never wrote), stops at one, and 'made herself look at the road'. No name is given. She frames her study as assessment (strengths in one column, faults in the other, for Antonidas).

beliefs.belief: She wants more than to assess it: she would give a great deal to see the keeping part work just once, and she wants the whole road on a bench under a good lamp with nobody in the room.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Admitted to herself, not to anyone else. Set against Garran eating it out of a bowl with a spoon; her body answers with nausea.

beliefs.belief: If she lays the case out clean, Arthas will move before Andorhal goes the way Millhaven did: he is quick, quicker than the courtiers credit, and hates being told a thing cannot be done.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: FALSE, overturned at Strahnbrad: he believed her and still did not move on it. See formerBeliefs.

beliefs.belief: Sylvanas has been too hard on a prince she never met; Arthas will look again, harder, because it is Jaina holding the paper.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: FALSE. She says aloud afterwards that Sylvanas was right.

beliefs.belief: Arthas was sure of himself before the fence, sure crawling back, and today sure before she finished and kind about it throughout. She asks whether she was unfair to a boy for years over one night (the band that fired the Garrow farm came out of those same camps with axes; 'perhaps the fences had been the right answer all along') and answers herself: 'No.'
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Left as her private verdict; the question is real and the orc dead are real, which is why she does not tell Sylvanas the story.

beliefs.belief: The tally-man was a tired clerk. She is not sure she tried: she had not turned the staff toward him, and she cannot read people anyway (she told Sylvanas so herself). The only reading off him was the road's drag, the same as the carters and mules.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Honest but incomplete. She does not connect him to the overseer or to the Millhaven carter beyond Sylvanas's remark, and she hates having come up empty.

beliefs.belief: Stopping to rest at the wall would be waiting on permission again; nobody behind her is coming (Arthas's letter will go north tonight; Antonidas does not know where she is). The city in front of her is the thing to ride at.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Her decision at the end of the chapter. Not tested yet.

beliefs.belief: Chapter 7: the poison is applied by hand, a thin coat worked through the grain after dressing and before the sack is sewn; alone it does little and what it carries wakes only inside whoever eats the bread (carrier layer at packaging, the body finishes the work). Whoever mixed it knows an alchemist's bench and necromancy, both.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Fits Sylvanas's sighting (arm in the sack to the elbow, protective gloves). Not yet contradicted. Stays on the Ch7-8 rung of her ladder.

beliefs.belief: Chapter 7: a live read is only possible while the loft is wet (gloves, bucket, boards round the crock); by morning she will have 'sacks again'. Speed is worth more than a proper arrest.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Operationally right; the capture is the test.

beliefs.belief: Chapter 7: she can freeze one man's jaw before he thinks to bite his collar, if she has her fingers on his skin, once tonight.
beliefs.trueOrFalse: Untested; Ch8 will answer.

formerBeliefs.belief: Soldiers want the short version; so she explains in small words to anyone who is not a mage.
formerBeliefs.why: Sylvanas had already ruled the lines on the map backward and found they close at Millhaven. Jaina recognises she was talking down to a woman a mile ahead of her and switches to the real register.

formerBeliefs.belief: Sylvanas is a cold obstruction who wants custody and the short answer.
formerBeliefs.why: Sylvanas listened, read the map, picked her ground and stood guard while Jaina went under; Jaina is 'glad of every one' of the escort by the crest, though she still hates being in the middle.

formerBeliefs.belief: Windrunner is 'maps': ground, ambush angles, ears sharp enough for a wolf in a holly wood; on people she has written her off ('A woman who said Mage. Up. and expected the mare and the mage to obey in the same tone').
formerBeliefs.why: In the lane Sylvanas gives up her bow, concedes Brask his point, speaks low and plain ('a woman telling him how far it was to the next ford') and turns his spear aside. Jaina concludes she was wrong and asks 'Could it be learned?'. She relapses at the chapel window ('gone straight back to thinking of her as maps') when Sylvanas reaches the granary and the flour on her own road; by dusk she brings the human side of the problem straight to Sylvanas ('Well, mage?' answered in full). Narration switches from 'Windrunner' to 'Sylvanas' at the window.

formerBeliefs.belief: The clean magical answer will be found by magic, and her best work is reading the body.
formerBeliefs.why: The staff-light shows where it is, 'not how it had got there'. She gets the route by asking the patients what they eat and having Tobin write on a slate (food, labour, timing), not by a spell. Antonidas 'could have stood at her shoulder and watched every step and had nothing to fault' though she did it by interview.

formerBeliefs.belief: Clear, ordered evidence plus rank and an old friendship will make Arthas act before Andorhal locks down; and Sylvanas is too cynical about the army.
formerBeliefs.why: She laid it out to him in order; he said 'I don't doubt you' and 'I believe you', and went back to the orc war (the Garrow farm). He never took the paper. Sylvanas called it in front of him before Jaina finished.

formerBeliefs.belief: Lordaeron's command is where rescue comes from (a letter to King Terenas, a council).
formerBeliefs.why: Arthas's offer is a letter tonight with his own rider and a visit once the hills are quiet. She sees that is waiting on permission again; she turns to Andorhal itself.

goalsAtChapterEnd.active: Be the one who gets her fingers on a living cultist tonight: freeze his jaw before he can bite, read Kett's loft while the residue is wet. Do it once.
goalsAtChapterEnd.underlying: Not shown on the page (Sylvanas POV); she has been writing nothing and talking while Corin wrote; she is spending what is left of her hands on the work.

goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter6.active: Ride down to Andorhal's market gate and ask at the militia post for Captain Havel, who the tally-man says knows the granary district; get inside and find who keeps the spread running; keep the staff, the pen-fingers and the sheet (now back in Sylvanas's coat) ready to show the thing to someone who can be made to see it.
goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter6.underlying: Stop waiting on anyone's permission or army; be the one who acts since nobody behind her is coming. Find out who built the thing (the face she stopped at and would not name). Not be the apprentice who was right too late.

goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter5.active: Ride the south road into the hills on her own read; hold the staff and the pen well enough to keep marking the map; be ready to 'show' the Strahnbrad soldiers the contamination when they block the way.
goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter5.underlying: Be useful in the Ranger-General's kind of hunt without pretending to rank in it; find where on the south road the thing goes in; stay on her feet. (Inferred: no interior this chapter.)

goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter4.active: Ride the grain road south and west after the young man with the cart (the staff leans toward the ruts); get the left hand good enough to tie a knot on her own hand, hold the staff and read again.
goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter4.underlying: Be a mage whose method includes what Sylvanas does (getting people to act) and what Lyriel taught (patching her own mistakes); understand the third part of the built contamination; find out who is good enough to build it.

goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter3.active: Stay upright, keep listening for the contamination down the road south, and be able to say which way it runs; heal the hands enough to read again.
goalsAtChapterEnd_chapter3.underlying: Be right, and not be the one who has to choose; hear 'which came first' rather than 'how loud'. (Her Ch2 wish to find someone alive in Millhaven was answered by the cellar; Sylvanas never saw that thought.)

emotionalStateAtChapterEnd.state: Outside view only: drained and grey to the lips after a day of reading every shelf in the sample room, but steady and plain; steps up beside Sylvanas before being asked and sets the staff down at her shoulder to face Havel; her fingertips went white at Corin's 'No.' to 'Did anyone answer?'

emotionalStateAtChapterEnd_chapter6.state: Hurt and spent in body (nosebleed, frost, pressure like deep water) and cold-clear in will. Angry at Arthas and at herself for expecting a second look; respectful of Sylvanas's read and willing to say so aloud, with no warmth spoken; haunted by a Dalaran face she will not name; stunned that Andorhal is working and the bread is still baking. Ends turned toward the city: 'The market gate.'

emotionalStateAtChapterEnd_chapter5.state: Seen from outside: exhausted, grey and frost-bitten but clear-headed and steady; no show of pride; laughs once in the dark wood; sits down without being told; says 'Then I'll have to show it to them.' (accepting the burden). Costly work: the fork reading leaves her teeth chattering and frost on her fingers. No interior.

emotionalStateAtChapterEnd_chapter4.state: Spent and shaking (sits the mare 'shaking all over' with her bandaged hand flat on its neck until it stops) but steadier than she has been: the village is alive, Elsie's forehead was cool on her cheek, her own knot held. Carries the guilt of Tam's death privately, a small bitter pang that the third part of the spell burned (and knows it was low of her), awe-and-horror at the craftsmanship of the thing, and a wary new regard for Sylvanas that she has not named. Holds no open trust.

emotionalStateAtChapterEnd_chapter3.state: Seen only from outside: exhausted to the point of sleeping in the saddle, nauseous and green when she listens, unembarrassed by saying 'I don't know', grim and steady; she follows the staff south without being told; she has dropped the formal pushing once the ground has overruled her. (Interior not shown.)

decisionsThisChapter.detail: Dropped the apology and the courtesies and told Sylvanas the blunt version first: necromantic residue in the leylines and the ward-stones, moving north and worsening.
Confessed that nobody sent her, the Kirin Tor do not know, and she left a note on Antonidas's desk; admitted to herself she kept the pebble wrapped so he could not tell her to come home.

Offered to prove it 'at a stone', and accepted Sylvanas's terms (inside the escort, hands visible, no stepping off the road, no touching stones unprompted) while asking for rangers because she would not be lucky twice.
Buried the pebble at the bottom of her satchel under stockings and field-book, 'and did not ask herself why the bottom'.

Asked to stop and lay a hand on the road on the hill below the outer stones; refused; asked again at the culvert and was granted it. Went down through the road into the clay and line and was pulled out after being called three times.
Explained the 'river over its banks' model; was corrected by Sylvanas; reframed the question as source or sink and asked to read at the crossing 'deeper than this morning'.
In the ambush: used the staff for a frost sheet that froze a wolf's hind legs to the road; stayed in the saddle.

Stepped off the road when ordered, read the doe through the hide, asked for the carcass opened, put her bare arm in to the wrist and beyond; reported the contamination is in blood, meat and organs and predates death.
Reached for her field-book slowly and visibly when Cyndia said 'Slowly'; wrote 'liver-roots-alive-before' with ink and blood.

Asked Sylvanas to let her read the crossing before full dark ('it's right under us'); was refused ('Houses first.') and obeyed, stopping a half-drawn gesture. Waited at doors where Sylvanas could see her hands.

Read the well with her left hand in the bucket water ('Thinner than in the doe'), then went down at the well-head with her left hand laid on the cobbles between two stones, listening to every line coming into the crossing at once ('further down than the culvert'). Asked to be called 'louder than last time'; had to be physically pulled out; left skin on the stones.

Reported the crossing test honestly: all lines heavy; two heavier far out than under the crossing (not rising); the two north lines lag by distance (suggests draining in); the east line does not lag; the west could not be heard, drowned by the crossing's thickness. Told Sylvanas 'I don't know... I can't tell you which way it's running.'

Pointed the staff worst toward the bridge and mill and 'under us, somewhere'; guessed the inn cellar. Climbed down into it with one hand and the staff, listened, and said 'Worse than the well. Worse again down by the mill.'

Read the storehouse with her left palm on the boards (frost spread further than at the well, dust going grey) and declined to call it the source: 'a store is where things end up'; accepted Sylvanas's order to stop reading with her hands that night.

Used the heel of the staff on the lane prints: 'It's in the prints... Heavier where they stepped than in the ground round them... The way it was in the doe.' Also checked the smooth bank for a baseline.

Descended the hatch at Sylvanas's order on her elbows and the heel of her good hand; checked the cellar for anything carrying contamination ('Nothing down here but her... Nothing that's been in here was carrying it'); kept the turnip heap between herself and the child.

From the wall of the room asked three of the useful questions of the child (sweetness before or after illness; how did you know she had died; which way the toes pointed; every night or one night) in a very low voice, and thanked the child for the shaving-glass answer.

Paid the Ch2 promise at night in the inn yard: listened at every horse with the heel of the staff (grey's tooth-score longest; Sylvanas's mare last) and said 'Clean. All of them. Tired horses, nothing else.'

At first light in the drove way, marked heavy versus light for every print, groove, wheel rut, hare and dog as Cyndia counted ('Heavy. Light. Light. Heavy.'), then sat down by the old gateposts and said aloud that the dead had not gone up 'our road'.

Opened her ink tin with her teeth and put it with a steel pen in front of Sylvanas when Sylvanas's lead stub failed ('Kirin Tor ink... They'll know that in Silvermoon.'); was told to put the lid back.

Stayed with Sylvanas (not sent north), rode in the middle, slept in the saddle, and at the gravel crossing at noon put the heel of the staff on the road and reported the contamination as 'thicker... wider, spread out... ahead of us... down the road.'

Entered the village noticing the drag under the market noise ('a blanket over a cough'); stopped herself from announcing 'necromantic' to Brask in front of the village; let Sylvanas handle the spear; went with Lyriel and Dickon to the chapel/infirmary.

Read the sick with the staff (Lyriel holds the crystal to the body through blankets; Jaina lays her cheek on the ash and sends the plain light word down): Elsie (fist under the breastbone, thread along the gut, nothing elsewhere), Garran (everywhere, every thread back to the gut), the cooper's boy and wife, Col, Wenna; also read a pump jug (thin, some in the water). Left the hands out of it, as ordered.

Used the holding ward (the first ward an apprentice learns, for flasks in a furnace) on people for the first time, on Wenna Dunmore mid-seizure, and then kept a rolling round of wards on every patient, trimming them before they guttered; Garran's took the most holding.

Retied Garran's bandage one-handed under Lyriel's coaching (loop over the thumb, wrist under, tail through, set it with the teeth); pulled out the knot Lyriel had tied for her and did it again; later tied the cooper's boy's dressing, and at dawn re-tied Garran's own bandage unaided.

Had Tobin write a slate of every patient: name, how long ill, how much she found, which well; then asked each what they eat. Built the bread answer (not water, not contact) and tested it against Mother Haw (oats, well). Stopped Tobin feeding Garran his sops and told him no store-flour bread for anyone.
Watched from the window above the altar while Sylvanas walked the granary and bakehouse; did not go down because the wards would thin.
Reported to Sylvanas in full register ('What sorts them is bread') and left the patients on Sylvanas's call ('Then we're quick') with the wards good to 'full dark. Perhaps a little after.'

Refused to stay by the water butt when told ('You won't know what you're looking at. I will.' by lifting the staff); went into the granary behind Sylvanas and Cyndia; pinned Tam to the floor with a frost cast when his sleeve came loose; threw a blue shell ward over the spilled substance to stop it reaching the sacks below; paid with a tear in the left palm and an iced arm.

Read the shelled substance through the shell against Lyriel's 'leave it' ('if she was going to pay for it she was going to have it'): same thing as in Garran, the doe, the Millhaven well, but whole and built; said aloud 'It's made. Somebody very good made this.'

Asked Tam 'Who made it?'; got 'I'm not to speak to you. You don't know what you're keeping them from.'; offered gentleness at the cage bars; knelt beside the dead boy and read his gut (clean: he had never eaten what he guarded).

Chose NOT to explain the stack and seams to Brask; went to Sylvanas instead: 'If the captain waits for the morning, they'll bake with it... I can ward a room. I can't ward a village.' Told Brask what to shut: granary, bakehouse, no baking or selling, and every sack of the man's flour in any house, 'I'm sorry, Captain. Every house.'

Ran back up to the chapel and kept the wards going all night; cooperated with Lyriel to rebind the hand; kept the shell-on-the-loft-floor report to Sylvanas ('Until morning. If nobody puts a foot on it.').

At dawn: checked Elsie's forehead with her cheek (cool); told Brask thank you for burning the loft boards despite minding; looked at the ANDORHAL sacking and said 'Then that's where his cart came from... Or where he wanted us to think it came from.'; spelled 'Proudmoore' for Brask's ledger; rode out on the grain road in the middle of the line.

Chapter 5: at Corley's yard picked the crossing over the yard to read from; read all four roads from a mile-post (north/west/south heavy and old, east light and starting); drew her marks on the waybill sheet with the pen in her two left fingers (blots, a cross like a bird's foot) and left her marks even when unhandsome; put a mark on Hollow Green from the bottom of its lane, then barred it and moved it to Brent's farm when Cyndia's book showed it was past it; at each crossing between stops got down (or was got down) and set the staff heel to read, said it to the ground; read the miller's yard ('Whatever was in the store has gone'), the river depot's barns ('thin... a room where somebody's smoked a pipe'), and the overseer (crystal at his chest: nothing on him); declined to claim she could read paper; told Sylvanas Barov ('One of the old houses... They hold the land round Andorhal, and the granaries.'); at the fork read the slips' places one at a time from memory of the roads (including 'You've had that', 'I haven't been there'); stepped out and set the staff between the two roads: the crystal's light leaned toward the south bend; corrected Ashford to heavy; offered a re-read at the first bridge and accepted the refusal; accepted 'Then I'll have to show it to them.'

Rode the south road through the mist reading the same late, dragging hitch under every bend (the road laid over something heavier than itself); recognised it as the hitch she felt at Millhaven kneeling in the lane with the staff heel in a dead man's footprint; fitted Corley's book, the slips, Garran's bowl, the jar made to keep and to wait, and Millhaven's walking dead into one reading; said it to Sylvanas in one plain line and admitted its gaps.
Decided to carry the whole case to Arthas, expecting it to move him; rode on toward Strahnbrad with the evidence.

At the hedge gave her name and title to the sergeant; took the folded sheet (with Barov slips and the sacking square inside) from Sylvanas's hand in her two bare fingertips; was lifted down by Lyriel; in the mud, met Arthas with the old teasing voice; gave him the case short and ordered (grain, made thing, mills and bread, Millhaven, the village south, depot slips, Andorhal at one end, the road worst), opened the sheet against the staff pinned by the thumb's knuckle; stayed careful on Barov; asked for men to shut the Andorhal granaries; was turned to face the valley and told about the Garrow farm; did not argue the orc dead; was left holding the paper, never taken.

Afterwards ran the internment-camp memory privately, judged him, asked herself if she had been unfair, answered 'No.'; let Sylvanas take the sheet ('Give it here, Mage.'); told Sylvanas aloud 'You were right. At the fork.'; did not tell her the camp story; thanked the lieutenant and declined the offered meal ('We won't be staying.'); said 'Andorhal.'

On the afternoon road she asked the tally-man (Sylvanas stopped him) for someone who would walk them round the yards and thanked him for Captain Havel; answered Sylvanas's 'Did you read anything off him?' with 'Nothing but a tired clerk'; when Sylvanas explained the farewell she said 'It's a farewell. Country people have dozens of them.'

Refused Lyriel's offer to get down and sit on the wall as the drag crushed in; let Lyriel steady the mare with a hand over hers; put her heels to the mare and rode on; reached the crest and called the destination: 'The market gate.'
Chapter 7: answers the gate clerk flatly under a Farstrider pass; when he starts to ask about the Ranger-General, cuts in 'My escort.' No cover name used.

Chapter 7: at the post, tells Havel about the tally-man referral; tells Corin nobody sent her; asks who he wrote to and whether anyone answered; asks about flagged-load samples and 'Can I put my hand on them?'; leaves with Corin and Lyriel for the sample room on the strength of Corin's magister's-ring access.

Chapter 7: reads every shelf in the sample room (offstage), tries to write the results and produces blots, then dictates them to Corin (Heavy/Clean per bag). Reports to the table: bags on copied marks are bad, bags on true marks clean.

Chapter 7: backs Sylvanas against Havel before being asked: asks what is left in the loft when the row is closed ('The crock. Where is the crock by the time your clerk gets there?'); gets up and sets the staff down at Sylvanas's shoulder facing Havel; says the loft is wet tonight and she can still read it there; offers to freeze the jaw of one man before he bites, once tonight, with her fingers on his skin ('Give me one close enough to touch.').

abilitiesDemonstrated.ability: Crossed two ward rings without anyone on the wall feeling her cross (reported).
Survey: hand-drawn human-paper map of the outer and second ring stones with ruled lines from the Lordaeron side to circled stones, creeks and the high road and Pass included.
Appears to hear or sense something wrong in a ward-stone that Sylvanas, from the doorway, cannot (frowns at the cell stone).

Hears the whole local current-field through stone, floor and staff: with the damper wedge pulled, every line in the Pass 'going at once'; a late, dragging pulse and an old-coin taste in the mouth mark the contamination. Can listen down the staff with its heel on the ground.

Deep reading by palm: goes down through road-crust, clay, groundwater, hedge roots and into the stone and the leyline beneath, tracking how contamination moves between them. Dangerous: she loses the hand and her sense of the surface; frost grows on the road around her palm (a hand's width, going grey when lifted).
Frost casting through the staff: a white sheet that cracks, spreads and glazes the road, freezing a wolf's hind legs to the hocks. Costs the use of her right hand.

Reads a living or dead body through the hide and from inside; locates the contamination at the liver, lungs, blood, meat; distinguishes ordinary death-cold (laid on from outside) from the contamination (running through the tissue like roots in a pot). Examines a horse's cut and finds hot horse, tired horse, clean blood.
Staff reacts to contamination: hums in the bones of her wrist, the crystal buzzes in its claws, rises as they near Millhaven, and points (shivers) toward the strongest source.

Chapter 3: reads a well (bucket water by hand), a crossing (every line's weight and arrival lag, to test source versus sink), a stone storehouse (floor, dust, frost spreading further than at the well), a cellar (anything carrying contamination?), a muddy lane (heavy prints against clean bank), a drove way (heavy versus light per mark, distinguishing cloven slot, dog pad, hare, wheel rut, and long drag marks), horses by staff-heel and cheek to the wood, and the open road at noon ('wider, spread out'). The crystal buzzes to a blur in the deep reads, rattles 'like a beetle in a box' at the storehouse, ticks 'tick on tick so close it nearly ran together into a hum' at the noon crossing.

Frost cost escalates: frost on a hand's-width at Ch2; at the well a white plate round her palm that reaches 'another finger's width toward the well' and tears skin off; at the storehouse the frost spreads further, 'the dust taking it and going grey'. Reading with the left hand alone is now the limit; Sylvanas bans hand-reads for the night.

Chapter 4 diagnostic light: says 'the word for light, the plain one, the first every apprentice in the Violet Citadel learned' and sends it down the staff 'water down a rope'; the crystal goes pale gold and lights a body from inside (organs, vessels, pulse) with the contamination showing brown 'like ink let fall into a glass of water'. Works with Lyriel holding the crystal against the patient and Jaina's cheek on the ash, because her hands cannot feel. The staff also ticks against its claws and her mouth tastes of copper when the drag is near.

Chapter 4 holding ward: blue 'cold clean blue, the shadow side of snow' mesh, put round living bodies; it takes the drag on each pulse like a line holding a tug and stops the spread, a cold running back up the ash into her elbow and chest. Stands on its own for hours, thinning; she has to feed and trim each ward in rounds. Taught in the Dalaran alchemy rooms for flasks in furnaces; she had never put it round a woman.
abilitiesDemonstrated.ability_note: Quickly improvised as a bowl-over-a-candle shell ward (a hard blue dome pressed to the boards, edges biting the wood) to contain the spill in the loft; it held until first light; it costs a tear in the palm.

abilitiesDemonstrated.ability: Chapter 4 frost cast on a person: pins Tam at the knees and free hand to the floor and the post's foot with white feathering frost (she had only done a wolf's hind legs before: 'A person made a different sound'); the frost thaws into his boots and he has no feeling in his legs for a while.

Chapter 4 reading the built contamination: can feel where the parts of a stack of spells meet (keep, wait, one she cannot follow), 'planking on a hull'; recognises it as the death-currents craft from the Dalaran signs (the grammar kept behind the grille) and reads every letter without understanding a word.

Chapter 4 diagnostic method (non-magical): slate-and-interview epidemiology (who, how long, how much, which well, what they eat), cross-checking against a healthy control (Mother Haw) and running ahead of herself and correcting ('Oats were grain too'). Good with a frightened sick room: names what she is about to do and what it will feel like.

Chapter 4 knots (new, Lyriel's teaching): one-handed bandage knot with a loop over the thumb root, wrist turned under, tail through, set with the teeth. Ties it on others by the middle of the afternoon, on a patient's arm unaided at dawn; cannot yet tie it on her own hand.

Chapter 5 road-listening: reads contamination off a crossing, a mile-post or a road surface, gauges age (old = settled in the ground; new = thin layer on top), and compares places without having visited ('I haven't been there'). Resolution good enough to rank four roads and to notice a nearer layer above an older one on the south road; she cannot read paper, books or people.

Chapter 5 new: the staff's crystal light physically 'leans' toward the contaminated direction at the fork (to the bend, the south road), a visible directional read she had not shown before. Costs: teeth chatter, frost on bare fingertips, cold draught that fills a room.
Chapter 5 non-magical: honest map-making, fast self-correction without pride (Hollow Green, Ashford); accurate noble-genealogy and politics (Barov houses, Boralus contract).

Chapter 6 synthesis: assembles supply-chain paper, a physical artefact (the jar) and a field read (Millhaven's prints) into one model of the plague as a built, distributed weapon, and tests it by deduction (rules out luck, fever, and a lone cart-driving wizard by what one man could not also have done). Recognises Dalaran-school design signatures (every seam closed) in a necromantic stack.

Chapter 6 road-sense: reads the drag with a late hitch through staff and mare on a moving ride; each farm lane that joins the south road adds 'a fresh thread of lateness' to it; the drag beats in the whole of Andorhal 'so much bigger than it had been all morning that she could feel it in the roots of her teeth'. Physical ceiling reached: frost on bare fingertips, nosebleed, crystal dimming to a stone grain.
Chapter 6 limits shown honestly: reads nothing off the tally-man (his residue is only the road's); has not turned the staff on him and admits it to herself; cannot read people.

Chapter 6 social: old courtly ease with Arthas (teasing, first names, Your Highness as a joke); formal self-introduction under a soldier's spear using Dalaran and Antonidas as her credentials; short ordered briefing to a commander; courteous deflection of an offered meal.

Chapter 7: reads sealed grain samples bag by bag as heavy or clean (every bag on a copied mark heavy; bags on true marks clean) while hours past a nosebleed; the cost shows as frost on the linen, white fingertips, a dead staff crystal and a grey face. Infers a hand-applied carrier coat from the readings plus Sylvanas's sighting.
Chapter 7: hand control: tries to write with two fingers, gets blots, and uses dictation instead (Corin's neat hand). Cannot read paper, so Corin carries the paper (Ch5 line stands).
Chapter 7 (stated, not yet shown): can freeze a living man's jaw with a fingertip touch, once tonight; 'I can still read it there' while the residue is wet.

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Jaina' aloud ('That man was paid by the loop, Jaina.'); no 'Lady Proudmoore'.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Cyndia (chapter 5)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: No name or title on page; helps her through a door and carries her to the gate.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Corley (chapter 5)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: None; hands her a cup of tea without a word.

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'the human' in the report; names her 'Jaina Proudmoore. Antonidas's apprentice.' howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'A woman. Mage.' / 'the human'

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Mage' as direct address throughout ('Mage. With me.', 'Mage. Up.'); 'Proudmoore' at the well ('Proudmoore.', '*Proudmoore!*') when she won't surface; in narration and thought 'the mage' in every chapter-3 scene, 'the prisoner' for custody. Never 'Jaina'.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Lyriel
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Lady Proudmoore' (dry, courteous, mildly teasing); chapter 3: no address on page, only helps her mount, takes her cheekpiece, holds the far stirrup.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Neral
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'My lady' (once, while checking her girth, chapter 2); chapter 3: 'a lady with a stick' (to the child) and the mage; no direct address.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Sylvanas
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: Chapter 4: 'Mage' in direct address ('Mage. What you find, I want before dark.', 'Well, mage?', 'Mage. Will it hold?', 'Mage. Up.'); to Brask 'my mage' ('let my mage see your sick'). Still never 'Jaina'.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Lyriel
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: Chapter 4: 'Lady Proudmoore' early (dry: 'Will you get down, or shall I fetch a ladder?'; 'If it bites me, Lady Proudmoore, I'm letting go.'), then 'Jaina' for the first time in mid-sentence during the knot lesson ('Go on, Jaina. Bite it. It won't bite you back.') and again at 'Jaina, leave it.' Jaina notices the first 'Jaina' at once.

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Miss' (as an afterthought), later 'the mage'; writes 'Jaina Proudmoore' in his ledger and has her spell it.

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Miss' (Dickon); Tobin uses no name ('Dalaran', 'Willem sent you?'); patients use none.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Arthas (chapter 6)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Jaina!' (laughing, on first sight), 'Jaina Proudmoore, on my hill', 'Jaina. I don't doubt you.', 'They came out of the camps, Jaina.' First name throughout, warm; says it before three elves and half his staff. Jokes 'Did Antonidas finally throw you out?'

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Sylvanas (chapter 6)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: Aloud: 'Proudmoore' in front of Arthas and the sergeant ('Proudmoore rides under my escort.', 'He's going to write to his father, Proudmoore'); 'Mage' otherwise ('Give it here, Mage.', 'Mage. Did you read anything off him?', 'Make it short.'). Never 'Jaina' aloud.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Lyriel (chapter 6)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Jaina.' aloud (once, at the nosebleed: 'Jaina. Your nose.'). No title.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Camp sergeant (chapter 6)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Miss' ('Everybody knows him, miss.').

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Granary tally-man (chapter 6)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: Addresses the party as a group; 'ma'am' to Sylvanas. No name for Jaina.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Sylvanas (chapter 7)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: Aloud: 'Proudmoore' in front of the others ('Proudmoore. The sample room. Take him.'); no 'Mage'. Interior (Sylvanas POV): 'Jaina' plainly, once 'the mage'.

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'My lady' ('Sit, please. You look done in.').

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: 'Lady Proudmoore', over-formal ('Proudmoore. Lady Proudmoore. From the— is it the Citadel?').

howOthersAddressHer.pattern: No address; reads 'Proudmoore, Dalaran, Kirin Tor' off the pass.

howOthersAddressHer.speaker: Lyriel / Cyndia (chapter 7)
howOthersAddressHer.pattern: No name or title on the page; Lyriel handles her without comment.

howSheAddressesOthers.pattern: 'Ranger-General' every time aloud, even when sharp ('Ranger-General, it's right under us', 'Ranger-General, a store is where things end up'). In her own narration (Ch2) 'Windrunner', 'the Ranger-General', once 'the elf', 'this soldier'.

Almost nothing said aloud; she nods thanks to Lyriel. Knows Cyndia's name from the passage; learns Lyriel's and Neral's from Sylvanas's orders. Chapter 3: speaks to no ranger directly except the child and Neral through the child.

Aloud: 'Ranger-General' (including the low request at the cage). Interior narration: 'Windrunner' (first scenes), then 'Sylvanas' from the chapel-window scene on, and 'Sylvanas Windrunner' once in the Millhaven-storehouse memory. Once thinks 'the egg stall... a woman who said Mage. Up.'
'Lyriel' aloud, first name, no title ('Lyriel. Bring me that jug.', 'Lyriel. The staff, please.'); asks 'Again' for the knot.
'Captain' (Brask, throughout); 'Tobin' (first name; he gives only 'Tobin'); 'Tam' (the lookout, 'Tam. Look at me. Slowly.').
Aloud: 'Ranger-General' ('Ranger-General.' to get her attention before the plain line; 'You were right' follows without title). Interior: 'Sylvanas' throughout.
'Arthas' aloud (a request, 'Arthas, I need you to listen to me'); 'Your Highness' once as a joke at first sight. Interior: 'Arthas'.
'Lieutenant' to the officer sent to feed them; 'sir' to the tally-man.
'Ranger-General' aloud ('Every bag on one of Corin's copied marks is bad, Ranger-General'); 'My escort' of her at the gate.

bodyLanguagePatterns.detail: Boots planted square, heels and toes, 'like a rider braced in the stirrups for a bad landing'. Hands flat on knees. Jaw clamped so hard the muscle shows under the ear.
Looks at Sylvanas's bow, quiver and colours, then her face last, a long careful read. Cocks her head at the cell stone like a hound at a rustle.

Draws her explanation in the air with both hands (lines, a river laid between the mare's ears) and has to be stopped mid-gesture; tucks the dead right hand into her armpit; sets the staff upright to listen; clenches her jaw and has to unclench it repeatedly.
Hides physical need (lets go of the chair back before anyone sees); hides her feelings behind a level voice while her ears burn; presses the stiff neck.

Chapter 3: starts a figure in the air with her left hand, stops, and puts the hand back down at Sylvanas's 'Houses first'; holds the stirrup leather 'not ready yet to let go of it'; sets the heel of the staff to listen and leans her ear or cheek to the wood; kneels and lays her left hand flat; sits back on her heels and holds the raw hand up to show it; leans on the staff; picks her way round holes in the lane; sits still against a wall with palms up; goes down into holes and cellars on her elbows; keeps a barrier (the turnip heap) between herself and a frightened child; sits at the far end of the settle from the child; lets her chin drop in the saddle and wakes with a jerk; stands with the stirrup leather in her fist until her legs hold; swallows twice when listening hard.

Chapter 4: shuts her eyes to hear the drag; leans forward in the saddle with her mouth open to deliver a speech and then closes it; lays her cheek on the ash to read, and on foreheads to take a fever; kneels with the staff pinned in the crook of the right arm against her ribs; sets the heel of the staff on the floor to push a frost or a shell; bites bandage tails; presses her bad hand flat on the mare's neck to stop shaking; stops breathing and clenches the reins until the raw fingers sing; holds the doorframe with the left hand (leaves a pale flour smear); looks up at the lit window; presses her face against the cage bars without knowing when; goes up Chapel Lane at a run holding her skirts in the dead hand; takes the bad-hand clean linen from Lyriel without arguing; picks at nothing, but sits down on the bench unable to remember sitting.

Chapter 5: stands with her back against a doorframe to rest and waits to be asked; sits down at the fork without being told; picks at frost on her fingertip with a thumbnail while reading the map upside down; leans on the staff's heel to rise; tucks the staff into the dead arm to take a pen in her left; drops her eyes shut at every crossing and says 'Heavy. Light. Old. Starting.' to the ground; lets Lyriel lift her onto the mare; holds a cup against her chest in the wrapped hand without drinking.

Chapter 6: goes still in the saddle at a realisation while the mare walks on; leans out away from Lyriel to spit; eases a clenched grip when the split pulls; squints into sudden sun on leaving the mist; lets go of the reins to take the paper with two fingertips; shakes the sheet open against the staff and pins the bottom edge with her thumb's knuckle; leans forward over the mare's neck to ask the clerk; blows at feathers on her hand; wipes her lip with the back of the wrapped hand; refuses to dismount ('No.'); looks to Arthas's retreating hair until the helmet goes on; grips paper until fingertips whiten; stays standing in the space he left until Sylvanas steps in; tries to refold the sheet with two fingers and fails; steps out ahead of an officer to refuse food before he speaks.

Chapter 7 (Sylvanas POV): leans forward on the staff to read bills; rubs two white fingertips together while explaining; fingertips go white on the staff at Corin's 'No'; stays on her feet by the bench rather than sit; turns on the staff with most of her weight on it; stops every few steps and lets Lyriel wait; sets the staff down at Sylvanas's shoulder to face Havel.

knowledge.detail: Has a hand-drawn map circling certain ward-stones (some twice), including the stone at the bend on the southern track. She ruled a line from each current she followed north to the stone where it ends. How she knew is unanswered.

Carries: sealed ink tin, oilcloth-wrapped pens, a swollen field-book, badly darned stockings (darned heels folded outward), hard bread, small brass compass, a straightedge ruler, and a flat grey pebble cut with a single rune wrapped in cloth (its twin sits in Antonidas's study; it has been silent since Dalaran).

Contamination: readable as late drag at the tail of each current pulse and an old-coin taste; thick in the ward-stones; muffled inside the Pass because the rings and the wedge stone in the cell hold it off (like a hand over her ear); worse outside the rings; has 'left the lines' and is in clay, water, hedge roots and living wood (a little, 'like salt'); is in the cabbage and bean fields, a doe's blood, meat, liver and lungs, and the empty farms; the Millhaven crossroads is a hard knot where every ruled line converges.

Knows from the culvert read, the fields and the doe that the contamination acts in living bodies before death and kept the doe moving after a heart-shot, but not how or how long ('longer than the fields back there have been rotting, I think').

Does not know whether it enters through food, water or air; the doe could have drunk it, eaten it with bark or lain in it. Does not know if the horses are infected beyond 'nothing I can feel'; wants to re-check tonight.
Knows the rangers' names: Cyndia, Lyriel, Neral; the fourth is unnamed. Does not know Sylvanas had felt a stone wrong at noon yesterday nor that Sylvanas had read her file.

Chapter 3: knows the contamination is in Millhaven's well water ('thinner than in the doe'), its storehouse (loudest), its inn cellar, its lane prints and the drove-way prints; that it is 'in everything here a little, and some things a great deal more'; that more is here 'than anywhere I've touched since Dalaran'; that the crossing read gives a mixed answer on source or sink; that the horses are clean again; that the dead walked a different way from the party's road; that the girl is not carrying it (cellar read). Heard the girl's account: sweet breath (pears gone brown) before fever, the baby, Mister Pell, the well, the glass held to Mam's mouth, the feet in the night, 'a new grain seller' cheaper than Mister Hollis, asked 'What grain seller?' and got 'The new one.' Was present (in the middle of the line) for the carter's grain-man question and Lyriel's answer; nothing on page shows her reaction.

Does NOT know (on page): whether the dead were alive when they walked ('I'd want one of them'), what the grain seller means, why the horses stay clean, how the sickness got into the village, whether anything leads the dead.

Chapter 4 knowledge: the contamination is taken by mouth in one flour; early cases are a fist (or a walnut) in the gut and a thread along the intestine; the late case (Garran) is everywhere (liver, lungs, great vessels, down both arms) and every thread runs back to the gut; sweet breath (brown pears) in the early/middle stages, going to 'meat kept too long' in the late case; water carries only a little; it is not passed person to person here. A stack of three spells in a clay jar with waxed cloth: keep, wait, an unreadable third. Recognises the death-currents craft from first-year Kirin Tor warnings (the signs, not the grammar). A young man with a cart brings the flour (and this is the same 'newer grain seller' as Millhaven, the girl's 'cheaper than Mister Hollis'): brown or fair hair, a good horse, civil, buys the keeper a jug. Granary lookout Tam died by poison from a sewn-in collar and said 'I'm not to speak to you. You don't know what you're keeping them from.' The sacks were stencilled ANDORHAL with a sheaf in a ring; Brask says Andorhal is the big granaries three days south-west by cart; she suspects it may be a decoy.

Chapter 4 does NOT know: who built the stack, what its third part does, who gives the young man the jars, who Tam's 'them' are, whether the contamination in the flour is also in the Andorhal granaries, how many more houses have flour, whether Mag (the flushed child under the egg stall) is already sick, why she is not herself ill despite the drag all around, how the same craft raises the dead (she has not yet seen a body rise from it).
Does not know (still): where Neral and the girl are or whether they reached the Pass; Jaina looks for Neral behind her in the line once and finds nobody.

Chapter 5: knows the contamination map across four roads (north/west/south old and heavy, east light and starting, King's road clean, south road worst and layered), Andorhal as the hub, the Barov name (lord of the court, holds land and most granaries round Andorhal), that she cannot read paper or people, and that the Strahnbrad army is on the south road. Backstory: Lord Barov visited Boralus once when she was small about a timber contract and talked about wheat all through dinner (father pretended to listen).

Chapter 6: knows the plague model (one thing made in parts, loaded by cart, baked into bread, accumulates, kills, walks) and its missing step; knows Arthas has seen and heard everything, believes her, and will send a letter north tonight and come to Andorhal when the Strahnbrad hills are quiet; knows a band 'out of the camps' with axes burned the Garrow farm (old Garrow, his daughter and her two boys; Arthas helped carry them out) and that his men's families live on farms in the line of the raiders; knows Sylvanas is carrying the sheet again; knows to ask for Captain Havel at the militia post just inside the market gate on the left (bench outside the door), and that the carts to the yards bear left at the bottom of the hill while the road straight on leads to the market gate; knows the King's road enters by a bigger gate to the right; knows from the rise that Andorhal is working (hoists, wagons, bake ovens, bell, mill wheel, a man singing) with the drag beating under it. Does NOT know: who built it; whether the face she stopped at is the builder; who runs Andorhal's spread; what Havel is; that the tally-man's phrase echoes the Millhaven carter beyond what Sylvanas says; that Sylvanas has turned the carter over since Ch5; why Sylvanas turned in the saddle so far.

Chapter 7: knows Corin's copied marks and sample-room bags (heavy/clean); that the sample room needs a magister's ring and that nobody has opened the bags; that Corin wrote weekly to the Citadel inspection desk and the Archmage's secretary and was never answered; that the poison is a hand-applied coat at packaging that wakes in the body; that the loft is wet tonight. Does not know whose hands. Sylvanas's roof account fills in the hands. She does not say what it means that Dalaran ignored Corin (her Ch6 private fear of a Dalaran-trained author is not voiced).

backstory.detail: Per the Farstrider file Sylvanas read last winter: a lord admiral's daughter, the archmage's favourite whom he brings to council, 'gifted beyond her years'.

Her father's crews and flagship supply her sea metaphors; she has ridden to King Terenas's autumn hunts; she was in the Violet Citadel at night with the lamp turned low so the porter would not see the light under her door, working out the hitch in the lines; the Citadel quartermaster gives cracked crucibles a once-over she recognises in Sylvanas.

Antonidas drilled her to clear her head and listen again over cold benches. Her left-behind note on his desk is the only notice anyone has. She came north alone and on foot by the sheep paths over the hills, and was lucky to arrive.

Chapter 3 (Sylvanas's view): Sylvanas recalls she crossed the rings on foot before dawn yesterday, sat in a cell all day with a damper in the wall, rode all night on a borrowed mare she couldn't sit, and put her hands into the road, a dead deer and a storehouse floor; she has been awake as long as Sylvanas, longer.

Chapter 4 (own memory): a flour mill on the quay at Boralus exploded the winter she was six; she was in bed and remembers her bedroom windows coming in. At eight she tied a bowline behind her back, with her father's bosun watching, for a bet; she knows a sheet bend, a clove hitch and the Kul Tiran gunners' breeching-rope knot. The little ones in the cathedral at Boralus stared at the reliquary when the priest carried it down the aisle (she was one). Her nurse took fevers by cheek on forehead. At the Violet Citadel in her first year apprentices are walked past the locked shelf of death-currents craft and taught the signs but never the grammar.

Chapter 6: the year she went to Dalaran her escort stopped for the night within sight of an orc internment camp. After the fire was banked Arthas scratched at her tent wall and whispered that she had never seen an orc, and there was a gap in the bracken under the watchtower nobody was watching. She said no; he said she was frightened; she went. They crawled on their elbows through wet fern; Arthas whispered the whole way that she would see beasts, that was why there were fences. At the fence she put her face to the gap between two stakes: orcs asleep by dead fires, and against a hut a female with an infant on her lap, its fist round one of her tusks, rocking it and humming. He was as sure at the tent door as before; she lay awake till morning thinking he could not see what was in front of him and never said so. She was a child, and so was he.

Chapter 6: in her first year at Dalaran a master stood under the locked grille of death-current books and told the room, in his fire-rules voice, that the whole art was keeping a body useful after the person in it had gone, which was why the grille was locked; somebody at the back laughed. She was taught to lay a ward with every seam closed. She has written up work for Antonidas as strengths in one column, faults in the other. She once dived off the end of the Boralus quay on a dare after a sailor's coin.

arc.lie: If she explains it clearly enough, any sensible person will act; and soldiers need the short version, so she talks small.
arc.truth: Sylvanas is a mile ahead of her on the map and the road; what she needs is the escort, and the real register works.
arc.currentPositionNote_chapter5: Chapter 5 (outside view only): the lie is effectively gone. She is no longer explaining at length; she gives one-word reads and corrects herself without pride, and Sylvanas uses her read to pick a road. She is still a prisoner of the Ch2 terms and not praised. The new beat: she accepts the next job ('Then I'll have to show it to them') and the road to be checked is hers alone.
arc.currentPosition: Chapter 4: lie weakened. She has the answer from food, labour and timing rather than from a clean spell, and brings the human side of the problem to Sylvanas instead of explaining louder; she watches Sylvanas's de-escalation and asks whether it can be learned. Not yet fully converted (she relapses to 'maps' at the window; still thinks in the Antonidas test). Her own craft costs her the left hand; Lyriel's knot gives her a small humble win. She is still a prisoner under the Ch2 terms in the middle of the line but is now the person Sylvanas asks 'Can you leave them?' and 'Will it hold?'.
arc.previousPosition_chapter3: Chapter 3: seen only from Sylvanas's side. Honest 'I don't know' under pressure and refusal to crown the granary mark her as someone who reasons by method, which is what earns Sylvanas's reluctant attention. She is still a prisoner in the middle of the formation, but she is the one Sylvanas hands the unreadable ground to and the one who 'knows where to go'. Her hands are the visible cost, and the cost is rising.
arc.currentPositionNote_chapter6: Chapter 6 (own POV): the lie 'clear evidence plus rank and history will move the powerful' is broken at Strahnbrad: Arthas believed her and went back to the war he can see. She concedes aloud Sylvanas was right (no history lesson given), and her anger turns outward. She now sees the plague as a deliberate Dalaran-school weapon and carries a private, unnamed fear about its author. The new turn: she stops looking north for rescue, refuses to rest at the wall, and rides at Andorhal itself. Still: 'Ranger-General' aloud; the camp story is kept from Sylvanas.
arc.currentPositionNote_chapter7: Chapter 7 (outside view; Sylvanas POV): goes out of sight on hostile ground with a stranger and returns with the half Sylvanas could not get; backs Sylvanas against Havel before she asks. Still 'Ranger-General' aloud. She will pay for the jaw plan with her last working hand.
